title: Tips to make more efficient use of Gemini 2.5 Pro for Unreal Blueprints game dev
author: DreamNotDeferred
selftext:
Hello all,

I have a middling understanding of AI in general and LLMs in particular, but I've been having a blast using Gemini 2.5 Pro in Ai Studio to guide me through developing a vertical slice for a game in Unreal Blueprints. I've wanted to make a game for decades, and using AI has gotten me further than I ever have toward reaching that goal. I've implemented several mechanics, that, so far, are all working together as designed.

However, once I got to \~500,000 tokens, I noticed a pretty high rate of hallucination and bad info, so I had Gemini compile a handover document to start a new chat. I edited the document a bit for clarity, and was able to successfully get Gemini in the new chat to have an accurate enough understanding of the logic in my project to keep working. Besides the handover document, I copy-pasted my blueprint logic into the chat, which used up a ton of tokens.

Perhaps I'm getting more familiar with Gemini, or maybe it's just anecdotal, but I feel like I'm seeing a fair amount of hallucinating at the 175-200k token mark in this new chat. Also, as a newbie game dev, the game logic is becoming complex and I'm having a hard time keeping track of it all mentally.

If I start another chat, I figure I'll probably lose 50-100k tokens just copy-pasting the current logic into the chat.

  
Anyone know of a better/more efficient way I can do this? Or anything I can communicate with Gemini to strengthen it's grasp of what I'm doing and minimize errors/hallucination in it's responses? I guess the larger question is does anyone have a workflow for something like this that scales well as a project grows.

  
Thanks for any help.

comments.author: Microtom_
comments.body: Gemini is much better with c++. It has a better knowledge of the API in cpp than its blueprint equivalent. You can also easily give it your files containing your classes.

replies.author: DreamNotDeferred
replies.body: So, I chose blueprints because I never got far trying to learn programming languages. When you say you don't need to know anything...how do you debug? How do you know what files to give it when starting a chat for a new feature in your game?

replies.author: Microtom_
replies.body:
I use jet brains rider IDE. It gives me debug messages when there's a problem.

First, I simply give the message to the AI. Usually that's enough.

If it isn't, I ask the AI to log each line with ue_log. There I give the logs to the AI. 

There are cases where it doesn't know something about the engine classes. I give it the relevant engine files. If it's too much information, I section the files and ask multiple times.

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: I started using Gemini and Chat GPT when I first started my game, but after about a month in it was clear they would only be of marginal help. Right now I only use them to look up nodes then I figure the rest out.

comments.author: nikosleft
comments.body:
I myself use Gemini as a "teacher" to help me learn to use blueprints efficiently in UE5. I don't agree with the other person saying to just switch to C++ and that you don't need to understand code. I think that actually getting to create the code yourself using blueprints and using Gemini as a "mentor" will aid you much more in the long run than just "copying" c++ files.

Either way here are things that help me;

1. Always ask Gemini to help you create comments for your blueprints/events/functions/etc. This way you never get lost.

2. Always stay under a 100-150k context window. Sometimes even less. It's best if you ask Gemini to help you create a "ProjectSoFar" txt file containing all of your Blueprints, events, code, bugs to fix, future game implementation ideas, in general anything that is important to your project. It is mandatory to update this project regularly (every day at the end of your session).

3. Don't go spiraling down a "troubleshooting" path if it doesn't resolve your issue in 2-3 tries. Chances are you didn't explain the problem well enough or simply you haven't yet even implemented the code that addresses the issue. 

Either way by working on BPs you will get real development experience that will help you understand C++ easier when you make the swap in your second project. In my opinion don't go into a scripting language since at that point you'll just be vibe coding.

If you have any questions you can shoot me a PM and we can hang out on discord and talk about our games.

Have a good one.

replies.author: DreamNotDeferred
replies.body:
Thanks for the reply. Yeah I definitely wasn't going the c++ no knowledge route; I'm strictly blueprints for better or worse. I've already been doing some of what you said; I've discovered that I've gotten to the point where I've been able to fix a few bugs and even implement a few simple mechanics on my own without the AI after working with it for a while, thank God. It's nice to see some growth after struggling to make even a basic game mechanic with traditional programming over the years.

I'll try the project text file arrangement that you mentioned, it still seems like it will eat up a lot of tokens as the project grows, but I'll give it a whirl. 

I would love the hang out and chat thing, if you were serious about that. Not sure how much help I could be to anyone else, but happy to try. I'll shoot you a PM later, thanks.
